title: The Buddhists you'll meet
hookLine: Theravada, Mahayana, Vajrayana, and many who simply sit: each a whole way

lines: A FULL MOON, A BLACK ROBE, BUTTER TEA.
cards: A potluck at a big-city Buddhist center, a little after noon. A Vietnamese grandmother quietly repeats the name of a Buddha under her breath. A Sri Lankan engineer mentions he'll be at the temple for the full moon.
A young woman in a plain black robe has just come from a Zen sit. A Tibetan family arrives with a toddler and a thermos of butter tea.
And a guy from the gym says he doesn't really call himself anything; he just sits every morning. They're all at the same table.

teach.h: THERAVADA — THE WAY OF THE ELDERS.
teach.b: Buddhists often speak of vehicles, yana, and you've now met all three. The Theravada, the way of the elders, in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia, with the Pali canon, the alms round and the full-moon days.
The Mahayana, the great vehicle, across China, Vietnam, Korea and Japan, with many schools inside it.
Pure Land Buddhists recite the name of Amitabha Buddha, trusting in his vow; that's the grandmother at the potluck.
Zen, called Chan in China and Seon in Korea, sits, and some of its lines work with the koans you met a few weeks back. Nichiren Buddhists chant the title of the Lotus Sutra.
The Vajrayana, the diamond vehicle, in Tibet, the Himalayas and Mongolia, with mantra, the teacher, and a day shaped by bodhicitta.
And then many who simply sit, in insight meditation groups or with a meditation app; some call themselves Buddhist and some don't. Here's what surprises newcomers.

In lay Buddhist life across Asia, meditation is often not the center of practice. Giving, keeping the precepts, chanting, bowing, caring for the monastery and the family dead: that's the practice, and it's a whole one.
Each of these is a complete way, with its own texts, teachers and saints. They disagree on real things, and they've learned from one another for centuries.

This path has tried to show each one on its own terms, and never to rank them. So when you meet a Buddhist, don't assume. Ask what their practice looks like; the answers vary more than you might expect.

how: Buddhists practice through Theravada, Mahayana (including Pure Land, Zen and Nichiren) and Vajrayana traditions, and lay Buddhists often center their practice on giving, precepts, chanting and devotion rather than meditation; others meditate in non-sectarian insight or mindfulness groups.

o: a stage of stillness reached in meditation
a school's founding scripture or main sutra
a vehicle: a tradition's own word for its path

games.q: at a gathering, you meet someone who says she's Buddhist. you've only learned about meditation. what's the best next move?
o: ask how long she meditates each day.
ask what her practice looks like.
tell her about your practice first.
games.why: don't assume. her practice might be chanting, giving, devotion or sitting; the answers vary widely.

practice: Bring back the potluck table, the grandmother, the engineer, the woman in the black robe, the Tibetan family and the guy from the gym, and silently wish each one well: may your practice go well.
Then wish the same to someone in your own life whose practice or faith differs from yours. Rest in the breath, which all of them share.

wordCard.voice: Yana. A vehicle: the word Buddhist traditions use for their own path, as in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali yāna: vehicle, as in Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna; Buddhist traditions describe their paths as vehicles.

carryVoice: Your line: many doors. Each one opens on a whole way of its own. See you tomorrow.
